lessonTitle: Heart Failure and Arrhythmia: Pump Failure, Neurohormonal Activation and Atrial Fibrillation

blocks.text: A 74-year-old woman needs three pillows to sleep, wakes at 2 a.m. gasping for air, and her ankles are so swollen that her shoes no longer fit. She has gained 4 kg in a week without eating more. Her ventricle is failing to move blood forward, so fluid is backing up into her lungs and legs while her kidneys, sensing poor perfusion, hold on to salt and water.

blocks.title: Heart failure
blocks.text: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of breathlessness, fatigue and fluid retention caused by a structural or functional abnormality of the heart that impairs ventricular filling or ejection, so that cardiac output is inadequate for the body's needs or is maintained only with raised filling pressures.

blocks.markdown: The pumping ability of the left ventricle is summarised by **stroke volume (SV)**, the blood ejected per beat, and **ejection fraction (EF)**, the proportion of end-diastolic volume (EDV) ejected. Cardiac output (CO) is heart rate times stroke volume. In the normal heart the **Frank-Starling mechanism** lets a greater filling volume produce a stronger contraction; in failure the ventricle sits on a flattened curve and extra preload yields little extra output but much more congestion.

blocks.caption: Ejection fraction. EDV = end-diastolic volume, ESV = end-systolic volume (mL).
Cardiac output (L/min) = heart rate (beats/min) x stroke volume (L/beat).

blocks.title: Calculating ejection fraction
blocks.prompt: On echocardiography a ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 80 mL. Calculate SV and EF, and say what this suggests.

steps.text: A normal EF is roughly 55-70% (laboratory and guideline variation exists), so 33% is markedly reduced and indicates systolic dysfunction.

blocks.answer: SV = 40 mL and EF about 33%, consistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

blocks.markdown:
### Reduced versus preserved ejection fraction

Heart failure is classified by EF. **Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)** has a weak, usually dilated ventricle (systolic dysfunction), typically EF of 40% or less. **Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)** has a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle that relaxes and fills poorly (diastolic dysfunction) while EF is normal, typically 50% or more; an intermediate group is sometimes labelled mildly reduced. Cut-offs vary slightly between guidelines.

### Neurohormonal activation

When output falls, baroreceptors and the kidney sense under-filling. Three systems are switched on. The **sympathetic nervous system** raises heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction. The **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)** is activated by reduced renal perfusion and sympathetic drive: angiotensin II constricts arterioles (raising afterload) and aldosterone retains sodium and water (raising preload). **Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)** is released and retains water. These responses are initially compensatory, restoring blood pressure and perfusion, but when sustained they are **maladaptive**: they overload the ventricle, injure myocytes and drive **remodelling** (dilatation and fibrosis), which worsens failure in a vicious cycle. Opposing them, the heart releases **natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP)** in response to wall stretch, causing natriuresis and vasodilatation, and BNP and its precursor NT-proBNP are useful blood markers.

blocks.title: Compensating for a low stroke volume
blocks.prompt: A failing ventricle has a stroke volume of 45 mL. To maintain cardiac output of 5.4 L/min, what heart rate is needed, and why is this a double-edged response?

steps.text: Convert SV to litres: 45 mL = 0.045 L.

The sympathetic drive that produces this tachycardia is helpful at first but raises oxygen demand and shortens diastolic filling and coronary perfusion time, contributing to progressive myocardial damage.

blocks.answer: A heart rate of 120 beats/min; sustained sympathetic activation is maladaptive.

blocks.markdown:
### Atrial fibrillation

**Atrial fibrillation (AF)** is the commonest sustained arrhythmia. The atria depolarise chaotically at 350-600 per minute and do not contract effectively. The atrioventricular node conducts only some of these impulses, in an unpredictable way, so the pulse is **irregularly irregular**. On the ECG, **P waves are absent** and replaced by a fibrillatory baseline, and the QRS complexes are narrow and irregularly spaced. It is associated with hypertension, heart failure, mitral valve disease, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol and ageing. Loss of atrial contraction reduces ventricular filling, and a rapid ventricular rate can precipitate or worsen heart failure.

blocks.title: The main complication of AF is stroke
blocks.text: Blood stagnates in the fibrillating left atrium, especially the left atrial appendage, and forms thrombus. Fragments embolise through the arterial system to the brain, causing cardioembolic ischaemic stroke. Stroke risk is reduced by anticoagulation, with the decision based on a validated risk score.

points: EF separates heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (weak, dilated ventricle) from preserved ejection fraction (stiff, hypertrophied ventricle).
Sympathetic, RAAS and ADH activation are initially compensatory but sustained activation causes fluid overload, remodelling and progression; natriuretic peptides provide partial opposition.
Atrial fibrillation shows absent P waves and an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm, and its main complication is cardioembolic stroke from left atrial stasis.

questions.stem: Which description best defines heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)?

options.text: Symptoms of heart failure with a normal ejection fraction and impaired ventricular filling
Symptoms of heart failure with an ejection fraction below 30% and a dilated ventricle
Right-sided oedema with a normal left ventricle and normal filling
Absence of symptoms despite a low ejection fraction

questions.correctOptionText: Symptoms of heart failure with a normal ejection fraction and impaired ventricular filling

distractorRationale.a: Correct: HFpEF is a diastolic filling problem with symptoms and an EF of about 50% or more.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: HFpEF is a disorder of the left ventricle with raised filling pressure, and is not defined by right-sided oedema alone.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: HFpEF is a symptomatic syndrome and by definition EF is not low.

questions.explanation: In HFpEF the ventricle contracts normally but is stiff, so filling pressures are high even though EF is preserved. The diagnosis requires symptoms and objective evidence of raised filling pressure.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction two years ago and now has exertional breathlessness. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle. Which classification and mechanism are most likely?

options.text: HFrEF from loss of contractile myocardium
HFpEF from concentric hypertrophy
HFpEF from restrictive filling due to ageing alone
High-output failure from anaemia

questions.correctOptionText: HFrEF from loss of contractile myocardium

distractorRationale.a: Correct: infarction replaces myocardium with scar, causing a weak, dilated, remodelled ventricle.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: concentric hypertrophy with a small cavity characterises pressure overload, not post-infarct dilatation.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ageing alone does not explain a dilated post-infarct ventricle.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: nothing in the history suggests a high-output state.

questions.explanation: A large infarct kills myocytes and the surviving ventricle dilates and remodels, giving systolic dysfunction with reduced EF. Ischaemic heart disease is the commonest cause of HFrEF.

questions.stem: Which hormone is released from ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch and promotes natriuresis and vasodilatation?

options.text: B-type natriuretic peptide
Aldosterone
Antidiuretic hormone
Angiotensin II

distractorRationale.a: Correct: BNP is secreted by stretched ventricular myocytes and opposes fluid retention.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: aldosterone retains sodium and water.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ADH retains water via the collecting duct.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: angiotensin II vasoconstricts and stimulates aldosterone.

questions.explanation: BNP is the counter-regulatory hormone of the failing heart, promoting salt and water loss and vasodilatation. Its blood level rises with ventricular wall stress and is used as a marker of heart failure.

questions.stem: Which ECG finding is characteristic of atrial fibrillation?

options.text: Absent P waves with irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes
Regular narrow QRS complexes with a sawtooth baseline at exactly 150/min
Progressive PR prolongation with dropped beats
Wide, bizarre QRS complexes with a regular rate of 180/min

questions.correctOptionText: Absent P waves with irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: chaotic atrial activity gives no discernible P waves and unpredictable AV conduction.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this describes atrial flutter with 2:1 block.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this describes Mobitz type I second-degree AV block.

questions.explanation: In AF the atria fire chaotically, so organised P waves are absent and the ventricles respond to a random fraction of impulses, giving an irregular rhythm. The QRS is narrow because ventricular conduction is normal.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with long-standing atrial fibrillation develops sudden left-sided weakness and facial droop. Which mechanism most likely explains the event?

options.text: Thrombus formed in the stagnant left atrial appendage embolising to a cerebral artery
Paradoxical embolus from a deep vein through the atria
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm because of rapid ventricular rates
Cerebral hypoperfusion from a fall in preload

questions.correctOptionText: Thrombus formed in the stagnant left atrial appendage embolising to a cerebral artery

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of atrial contraction produces stasis and thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage, which can embolise.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: paradoxical embolism requires a right-to-left shunt and is not the mechanism in AF.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: AF does not cause berry aneurysm rupture.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: haemodynamic hypoperfusion would not give a focal deficit of sudden onset in this way.

questions.explanation: Fibrillating atria do not empty, so blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage and clots. These emboli travel to the brain, which is why stroke is the principal complication and why anticoagulation is used.

questions.stem: Echocardiography of a 66-year-old woman shows an end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and an end-systolic volume of 60 mL. Calculate her left ventricular ejection fraction as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is 150 - 60 = 90 mL, and EF = 90 / 150 = 0.60, or 60%. A normal EF with symptoms of congestion would point to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic heart failure has a stroke volume of 55 mL and a heart rate of 96 beats/min. Calculate cardiac output in L/min.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output is HR x SV = 96 x 55 mL = 5280 mL/min, which is 5.28 L/min. Sympathetic activation raises heart rate to maintain output when stroke volume is reduced.

questions.stem: Compare heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in terms of defect, ventricular structure, ejection fraction and typical causes.
markingGuide: HFrEF: systolic dysfunction, weak dilated ventricle, EF about 40% or less
HFpEF: diastolic dysfunction, stiff hypertrophied ventricle, EF about 50% or more
HFrEF causes: myocardial infarction, dilated cardiomyopathy
HFpEF causes: hypertension, ageing, diabetes, obesity
Both can present with symptoms and signs of congestion and raised natriuretic peptides
questions.explanation: The two syndromes differ in whether the primary problem is impaired contraction or impaired relaxation and filling. EF is the pragmatic measure that separates them, but both present with similar congestive symptoms.

questions.stem: Explain why neurohormonal activation helps in acute heart failure but worsens chronic heart failure. Refer to the sympathetic nervous system, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH, and name one counter-regulatory hormone.
markingGuide: Triggered by reduced cardiac output and renal perfusion sensed by baroreceptors and kidney
Sympathetic activation: raised heart rate and contractility and vasoconstriction maintain pressure
RAAS: angiotensin II vasoconstriction raises afterload; aldosterone retains salt and water raising preload
Chronic effects: congestion, increased myocardial oxygen demand, remodelling (dilatation, fibrosis), progression
Counter-regulatory: ANP or BNP causing natriuresis and vasodilatation
questions.explanation: These responses restore perfusion pressure when output drops, which is beneficial in the short term. Sustained activation overloads and injures the ventricle and drives remodelling, creating a vicious cycle that is the rationale for RAAS blockade and beta-blockade.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has an irregular pulse. Describe the ECG features that confirm atrial fibrillation, explain why the pulse is irregular, and explain how the arrhythmia causes its main complication.
markingGuide: ECG: absent P waves with fibrillatory baseline
Chaotic atrial activity at 350-600/min with variable conduction through the AV node
Loss of effective atrial contraction leads to stasis in the left atrial appendage
Thrombus formation and embolisation causes cardioembolic ischaemic stroke
questions.explanation: The atrioventricular node filters the chaotic atrial impulses so that ventricular activation is random in timing. Stasis in the non-contracting atrium promotes clot, and emboli to the brain cause stroke.
